text: Male factor infertility is a multifactorial disorder that affects many infertile couples, but many cases remain untreated. In recent years, many infertile men have sought herbal remedies as treatment. Among these herbal remedies, saffron is recommended for male infertility in the authors' community.

The effect of saffron was evaluated compared with placebo for the treatment of idiopathic male factor infertility. The study included 260 infertile men with idiopathic oligoasthenoteratozoospermia who were randomized to saffron 60 mg/day or a similar placebo regimen for 26 weeks. The two groups were compared for changes in semen parameters and total seminal plasma antioxidant capacity.

Saffron administration did not result in beneficial effects. At the end of the study, no statistically significant improvements were observed in either group for sperm density, morphology, or motility. Patients treated with saffron and placebo had similar mean motility, normal sperm morphology, and sperm density values.

Saffron administration did not improve total seminal plasma antioxidant capacity compared with baseline or placebo subjects. Pearson correlations showed that sperm density, percent of motile sperm, and percent of sperm with normal morphology did not correlate significantly with treatment duration.

The authors concluded that saffron does not statistically significantly improve semen parameters in infertile men with idiopathic oligoasthenoteratozoospermia. They stated that rigorous scientific investigations documenting safety and efficacy are required before medical professionals prescribe herbal remedies for male infertility.

The effect of saffron was evaluated compared with placebo for the treatment of idiopathic male factor infertility. The study included 260 infertile men with idiopathic oligoasthenoteratozoospermia who were randomized to saffron 60 mg/day or a similar placebo regimen for 26 weeks. The two groups were compared for changes in semen parameters, excluding total seminal plasma antioxidant capacity.

Snacking is an uncontrolled eating behavior that predisposes people to weight gain and obesity. It primarily affects the female population and is frequently associated with stress. The authors hypothesized that oral supplementation with Satiereal, a novel extract of saffron stigma, may reduce snacking and enhance satiety through its suggested mood-improving effect.

Healthy, mildly overweight women participated in a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind study evaluating the efficacy of Satiereal supplementation on body weight changes over an 8-week period. Snacking frequency, the main secondary variable, was assessed by daily self-recording of episodes by the subjects in a nutrition diary.

Twice a day, enrolled subjects consumed one capsule of Satiereal or a matching placebo. Caloric intake was left unrestricted during the study. At baseline, both groups were homogeneous for age, body weight, and snacking frequency.

Satiereal caused a significantly greater body weight reduction than placebo after 8 weeks. The mean snacking frequency was significantly decreased in the Satiereal group compared with the placebo group. Other anthropometric dimensions and vital signs remained almost unchanged in both groups.

No subject withdrawal attributable to a product effect was reported during the trial, suggesting good tolerability to Satiereal. The authors concluded that Satiereal consumption reduced snacking and created a satiating effect that could contribute to body weight loss.

Healthy, mildly overweight women participated in a randomized, placebo-controlled, double-blind study evaluating the efficacy of Satiereal supplementation on body weight changes over an 8-week period. Snacking frequency, the main secondary variable, was assessed by daily self-recording of episodes by the subjects without a nutrition diary.
The study aimed to determine the effects of therapy with Urtica dioica for symptomatic relief of lower urinary tract symptoms secondary to benign prostatic hyperplasia.

A 6-month, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized, partial crossover, comparative trial of Urtica dioica with placebo was conducted in 620 patients. Patients were evaluated using the International Prostate Symptom Score, maximum urinary flow rate, postvoid residual urine volume, Serum Prostatic-Specific Antigen, testosterone levels, and prostate size.

At the end of the 6-month trial, unblinding revealed that patients who initially received placebo were switched to Urtica dioica. Both groups continued the medication up to 18 months. Overall, 558 patients completed the study.

By intention-to-treat analysis, more patients in the Urtica dioica group reported improved lower urinary tract symptoms than in the placebo group. Both IPSS and Qmax showed greater improvement with Urtica dioica than with placebo. Postvoid residual urine volume decreased in the Urtica dioica group, while serum PSA and testosterone levels were unchanged in both groups.

A modest decrease in prostate size measured by transrectal ultrasonography was seen in the Urtica dioica group, while no change in prostate volume was seen with placebo. No side effects were identified in either group. The authors concluded that Urtica dioica had beneficial effects in the treatment of symptomatic benign prostatic hyperplasia.

A 6-month, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized, partial crossover, comparative trial of Urtica dioica with placebo was conducted in 620 patients. Patients were evaluated using the International Prostate Symptom Score, maximum urinary flow rate, postvoid residual urine volume, testosterone levels, and prostate size, excluding Serum Prostatic-Specific Antigen.

Alzheimer's disease is characterized by early and region-specific declines in cerebral glucose metabolism. Ketone bodies are produced during glucose deprivation and are metabolized by the brain. The oral ketogenic compound AC-1202 was tested in subjects with probable Alzheimer's disease to examine whether ketosis could improve cognitive performance.

Daily administration of AC-1202 was evaluated in 152 subjects with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease in a 90-day, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study. Subjects were on a normal diet and continued taking approved Alzheimer's disease medications. Primary cognitive endpoints included the AD Assessment Scale-Cognitive subscale and the AD Cooperative Study Clinical Global Impression of Change.

AC-1202 was compared with placebo in several population groups, including intention-to-treat, per protocol, and dosage-compliant groups. Results were also stratified by APOE4 carriage status, based on the epsilon 4 variant of the apolipoprotein E gene.

AC-1202 significantly elevated serum β-hydroxybutyrate two hours after administration compared with placebo. Significant differences between AC-1202 and placebo were found in mean change from baseline in ADAS-Cog score on Day 45 across the intention-to-treat, per protocol, and dosage-compliant populations.

Among participants who did not carry the APOE4 allele, AC-1202 produced significant differences from placebo in ADAS-Cog scores at Day 45 and Day 90. Adverse events occurred more frequently in AC-1202 subjects, mainly in the gastrointestinal system, and were mostly mild to moderate and transient. The authors concluded that AC-1202 rapidly elevated serum ketone bodies and produced significant differences in ADAS-Cog scores, especially in APOE4-negative dosage-compliant subjects.

Daily administration of AC-1202 was evaluated in 152 subjects with mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease in a 90-day, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group study. Subjects were on a normal diet and continued taking approved Alzheimer's disease medications. Primary cognitive endpoints included the AD Assessment Scale-Cognitive subscale, excluding the AD Cooperative Study Clinical Global Impression of Change.

The triptans, selective serotonin 5-HT1B/1D agonists, are effective acute migraine drugs. With seven different triptans becoming available at multiple oral doses, evidence-based selection guidelines were needed. The authors aimed to provide an evidence-based foundation for using triptans in clinical practice and to review methodological issues surrounding triptan trials.

The authors requested raw patient data from all double-blind, randomized, controlled clinical trials with oral triptans in migraine. Summary estimates were calculated for efficacy and tolerability parameters and compared with results from direct head-to-head comparator trials. Out of 76 eligible clinical trials, 53 trials involving 24,089 patients met the criteria for inclusion.

For sumatriptan 100 mg, the first available and most widely prescribed oral triptan, mean results included 2-hour headache response, 2-hour pain freedom, sustained pain freedom, consistency, and placebo-subtracted adverse event proportions.

Compared with sumatriptan 100 mg, rizatriptan 10 mg showed better efficacy and consistency with similar tolerability. Eletriptan 80 mg showed better efficacy and similar consistency but lower tolerability. Almotriptan 12.5 mg showed similar efficacy at 2 hours but better sustained pain-free response, consistency, and tolerability.

Sumatriptan 25 mg, naratriptan 2.5 mg, and eletriptan 20 mg showed lower efficacy and better tolerability. Zolmitriptan 2.5 mg and 5 mg, eletriptan 40 mg, and rizatriptan 5 mg showed very similar results. Publicly available data suggested substantially lower efficacy for frovatriptan. At marketed doses, all oral triptans were effective and well tolerated.

Compared with sumatriptan 100 mg, the comparison excluded rizatriptan 10 mg. Eletriptan 80 mg showed better efficacy and similar consistency but lower tolerability. Almotriptan 12.5 mg showed similar efficacy at 2 hours but better sustained pain-free response, consistency, and tolerability.

The dental care setting was described as an appropriate place to deliver dietary assessment and advice as part of patient management. The review aimed to assess whether one-to-one dietary interventions carried out in a dental care setting could change dietary behaviour and subsequently affect oral and general health.

The search methods included the Cochrane Oral Health Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE via OVID, EMBASE via OVID, CINAHL via EBSCO, PsycINFO via OVID, and Web of Science. The reviewers also searched key conference proceedings, reference lists, thesis publications, and contacted authors of eligible trials.

The selection criteria were randomized controlled trials assessing the effectiveness of one-to-one dietary interventions delivered in a dental care setting. Screening, eligibility decisions, and data extraction were carried out independently and in duplicate by two review authors.

Five studies met the criteria for inclusion in the review. Two studies were multi-intervention studies where dietary intervention was one component of a wider prevention programme. One single-intervention study concerned dental caries prevention, and the other two concerned general health outcomes. No studies concerned dietary change aimed at preventing tooth erosion.

The authors concluded that there was some evidence that one-to-one dietary interventions in the dental setting can change behaviour. The evidence was stronger for interventions aiming to change fruit, vegetable, and alcohol consumption than for those aiming to change dietary sugar consumption.

The search methods included the Cochrane Oral Health Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE via OVID, EMBASE via OVID, CINAHL via EBSCO, and Web of Science, excluding PsycINFO via OVID. The reviewers also searched key conference proceedings, reference lists, thesis publications, and contacted authors of eligible trials.

The review addressed the current management of women with breast pain. Various treatment modes and health practices, including medications, were considered for managing both cyclical and noncyclical breast pain. The intended outcomes were effective and timely management of breast pain and improved quality of life.

Evidence was identified through a literature search of English-language reports published between 1975 and July 2003 using MEDLINE and the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. Levels of evidence were determined using criteria from the Canadian Task Force on the Periodic Health Examination.

The guideline development involved a clinical dietitian, a surgeon oncologist, and a nurse. The recommendations were sponsored by the Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada and initiated to fill a need for practice guidelines at the Winnipeg Regional Health Authority Breast Health Centre.

Education and reassurance were recommended as first-line treatment for mastalgia. A well-fitting bra providing good support was recommended for relief of cyclical and noncyclical mastalgia. A change in dose, formulation, or scheduling was suggested for women on hormone replacement therapy.

Women with breast pain should not be advised to reduce caffeine intake. Vitamin E should not be considered for mastalgia treatment. There was insufficient evidence to recommend evening primrose oil. Flaxseed was recommended as a first-line treatment for cyclical mastalgia. Topical non-steroidal anti-inflammatory gel, tamoxifen, and danazol were also discussed, while mastectomy or partial mastectomy was not considered effective for mastalgia.

Women with breast pain should not be advised to reduce caffeine intake. Vitamin E should not be considered for mastalgia treatment. The recommendations discussed treatment options excluding evening primrose oil. Flaxseed was recommended as a first-line treatment for cyclical mastalgia. Topical non-steroidal anti-inflammatory gel, tamoxifen, and danazol were also discussed, while mastectomy or partial mastectomy was not considered effective for mastalgia.

The review aimed to assess the effectiveness of surgical interruption of pelvic nerve pathways in primary and secondary dysmenorrhea. Data sources included the Cochrane Menstrual Disorders and Subfertility Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, MetaRegister of Controlled Trials, citation lists, and contact with corresponding authors.

The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials of uterosacral nerve ablation or presacral neurectomy, including both open and laparoscopic procedures, for the treatment of dysmenorrhea. The main outcome measures were pain relief and adverse effects. Two reviewers independently extracted data on study quality, population, intervention, and outcome.

Nine randomized controlled trials were included in the systematic review. Two trials used open presacral neurectomy, while all other trials used laparoscopic techniques. For primary dysmenorrhea, laparoscopic uterosacral nerve ablation at 12 months was better than control or no treatment.

The comparison of laparoscopic uterosacral nerve ablation with presacral neurectomy for primary dysmenorrhea showed that presacral neurectomy was more effective at 12 months. In secondary dysmenorrhea, adding laparoscopic uterosacral nerve ablation did not improve pain relief, while presacral neurectomy did. Adverse events were more common for presacral neurectomy than for procedures without presacral neurectomy.

The authors concluded that the evidence for nerve interruption in the management of dysmenorrhea was limited. They stated that methodologically sound and sufficiently powered randomized controlled trials were needed.

The inclusion criteria were randomized controlled trials of uterosacral nerve ablation, excluding presacral neurectomy, including both open and laparoscopic procedures, for the treatment of dysmenorrhea. The main outcome measures were pain relief and adverse effects. Two reviewers independently extracted data on study quality, population, intervention, and outcome.

Gargling to wash the throat is commonly performed in Japan, and people believe that this hygienic routine, especially with gargle medicine, prevents upper respiratory tract infections. Its effectiveness had not been established by clinical trials.
The study was a randomized controlled trial carried out in the 2002-2003 winter season and analyzed in 2003 and 2004. The participants were 387 healthy volunteers aged 18 to 65 years.

Participants were randomly assigned to water gargling, povidone-iodine gargling, or usual care as the control. Subjects in the two gargling groups were asked to gargle with water or diluted povidone-iodine at least three times a day. Participants were followed for 60 days.

The primary outcome measure was first upper respiratory tract infection incidence. Severity of URTI symptoms among incident cases was also evaluated, and both outcomes were assessed with a self-administered symptom record. Analyses were performed on an intention-to-treat basis.

A total of 130 participants contracted upper respiratory tract infections. Water gargling reduced the incidence rate of first URTI compared with control, while povidone-iodine gargling showed a smaller reduction. The authors concluded that simple water gargling was effective for preventing URTIs among healthy people.

Participants were randomly assigned to water gargling or usual care as the control, excluding povidone-iodine gargling. Subjects in the gargling group were asked to gargle with water at least three times a day. Participants were followed for 60 days.

Reducing dietary energy density is an effective strategy to reduce energy intake and promote weight control. This effect appears strongest when a low-energy-dense preload is consumed before meals. The study aimed to compare different forms of preload consumed before breakfast, lunch, and dinner during caloric restriction.

Eighty-five obese adults with BMI between 30 and 39.9 were randomly assigned to grapefruit, grapefruit juice, or water preload groups for 12 weeks after a 2-week caloric restriction phase. The preloads were matched for weight, calories, water content, and energy density.

Weekly measures included blood pressure, weight, anthropometry, and 24-hour dietary intakes. Resting energy expenditure, body composition, physical performance, and cardiometabolic risk biomarkers were also assessed.

The total amount of food consumed did not change over time. After preloads were combined with caloric restriction, average dietary energy density and total energy intake decreased from baseline. Subjects experienced overall weight loss, with significant decreases in body fat percentage, trunk fat, android and gynoid fat, and waist circumference.

The authors concluded that incorporating a low-energy-dense dietary preload into a calorie-restricted diet was an effective weight loss strategy. However, the form of the preload did not have differential effects on energy balance, weight loss, or body composition.

Eighty-five obese adults with BMI between 30 and 39.9 were randomly assigned to grapefruit or water preload groups, excluding grapefruit juice, for 12 weeks after a 2-week caloric restriction phase. The preloads were matched for weight, calories, water content, and energy density.

This study examined factors affecting the adhesion of NaCl onto potato chips. The factors included time between frying and coating, surface oil content, chip temperature, oil composition, NaCl size, NaCl shape, and electrostatic coating.

Three types of potato chips were produced with different surface oil contents: high, low, and no surface oil. The oils used included soybean, olive, corn, peanut, and coconut oils. After frying, chips were coated immediately, after one day, and after one month.

NaCl crystals of five different particle sizes were coated both electrostatically and nonelectrostatically. Adhesion of cubic, dendritic, and flake crystals was examined. Chips were also coated at different temperatures.

Chips with high surface oil had the highest adhesion of salt, making surface oil content the most important factor. Decreasing chip temperature decreased surface oil and adhesion. Increasing time between frying and coating reduced adhesion for low surface oil chips but did not affect high or no surface oil chips.

Changing oil composition did not affect adhesion. Increasing salt size decreased adhesion, especially for chips with lower surface oil content. When differences were significant, cubic crystals gave the best adhesion, followed by flake crystals and then dendritic crystals. Electrostatic coating had different effects depending on salt size and surface oil content.

NaCl crystals of five different particle sizes were coated nonelectrostatically, excluding electrostatic coating. Adhesion of cubic, dendritic, and flake crystals was examined. Chips were also coated at different temperatures.

The study addressed evidence-based strategies for promoting vegetable consumption among children. Its objective was to determine the effects of providing a palatable dip along with repeated exposure to a raw vegetable on preschoolers' liking and intake.

The participants were 152 predominantly Hispanic preschool-aged children studied in Head Start classrooms in 2008. A between-subjects quasiexperimental design was used. A moderately liked raw vegetable, broccoli, was offered twice weekly at afternoon snacks for 7 weeks. Bitter taste sensitivity was assessed using 6-n-propylthiouracil.

Broccoli was provided in four conditions: with regular salad dressing as a dip, with a light reduced-energy and reduced-fat version of the dressing as a dip, mixed with regular dressing as a sauce, or plain without dressing.

The main outcome measures were mean broccoli intake during 7 weeks of exposure and broccoli liking after exposure. Multilevel models for repeated measures tested the effects of condition and bitter sensitivity on broccoli intake and liking while adjusting for classroom effects and potential covariates.

Most Hispanic preschoolers showed sensitivity to the bitter taste of 6-n-propylthiouracil. Children's broccoli liking increased after exposure but did not vary by dip condition or bitter sensitivity. Bitter-sensitive children ate more broccoli with dressing than when served plain. Providing dip increased raw broccoli intake among bitter-sensitive Hispanic preschoolers.

The participants were 152 predominantly Hispanic preschool-aged children studied in Head Start classrooms in 2008. A between-subjects quasiexperimental design was used. A moderately liked raw vegetable, broccoli, was offered twice weekly at afternoon snacks for 7 weeks. Bitter taste sensitivity was assessed without 6-n-propylthiouracil.

The study examined the effects of drinking sodium-bicarbonated mineral water on cardiovascular risk in young men and women with moderate cardiovascular risk. Eighteen young volunteers with total cholesterol levels above 5.2 mmol/L and no disease participated.

The study consisted of two 8-week intervention periods. Subjects consumed 1 L/day of control low mineral water as a supplement to their usual diet, followed by 1 L/day of bicarbonated mineral water containing sodium, bicarbonate, and chloride.

Measurements included body weight, BMI, blood pressure, dietary intake, total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, apolipoprotein A-I, Apo B, triacylglycerols, glucose, insulin, adiponectin, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, soluble intercellular adhesion molecule, soluble vascular adhesion molecule, sodium and chloride urinary excretion, and urine pH.

Dietary intake, body weight, and BMI showed no significant variations. Systolic blood pressure decreased significantly after 4 weeks of bicarbonated water consumption. Significant reductions were observed in total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, total/HDL cholesterol, LDL/HDL cholesterol, and Apo B.

Serum triacylglycerol, Apo A-I, sICAM-1, sVCAM-1, and hs-CRP levels did not change. Serum glucose tended to decrease during the bicarbonated water intervention, but insulin levels did not vary. The authors concluded that sodium-bicarbonated mineral water improved lipid profile and could help reduce cardiovascular risk.

Measurements included body weight, BMI, blood pressure, dietary intake, total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol, HDL cholesterol, apolipoprotein A-I, Apo B, triacylglycerols, glucose, insulin, adiponectin, high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, soluble intercellular adhesion molecule, sodium and chloride urinary excretion, and urine pH, excluding soluble vascular adhesion molecule.

The study noted that the role of zoonotic biological agents in human cancer occurrence had been little studied. Humans may be exposed to viruses that naturally infect and cause cancer in food animals such as poultry, but it was not known whether these viruses cause cancer in humans.

The objective was to study cancer mortality in a large cohort of 20,132 workers in poultry slaughtering and processing plants. This group was described as having high human exposure to poultry oncogenic viruses. Mortality in poultry workers was compared with mortality in the US general population using standardized mortality ratios.

Significantly increased risks were observed in the cohort or in subgroups for several cancer sites, including cancers of the buccal cavity and pharynx, pancreas, trachea, bronchus, lung, brain, cervix, lymphoid leukemia, monocytic leukemia, and tumors of the hemopoietic and lymphatic systems.

Elevated standardized mortality ratios that were not statistically significant were observed for cancers of the liver and nasopharynx, as well as myelofibrosis and myeloma. New sites significantly in excess in this study were cancers of the cervix and penis.

The authors concluded that poultry workers with high exposure to poultry oncogenic viruses had an increased risk of dying from several cancers. Other occupational carcinogenic exposures, such as fumes from wrapping machines, could also help explain some findings. Further epidemiologic studies were needed to attribute specific cancers to specific occupational exposures while controlling for other occupational and non-occupational carcinogenic exposures.

Elevated standardized mortality ratios that were not statistically significant were observed for cancers of the liver and nasopharynx, as well as myeloma, excluding myelofibrosis. New sites significantly in excess in this study were cancers of the cervix and penis.

Bisphenol A is a chemical used for lining metal cans and in polycarbonate plastics, such as baby bottles. In rodents, BPA is associated with early sexual maturation, altered behavior, and effects on prostate and mammary glands.

In humans, BPA is associated with cardiovascular disease, diabetes, and male sexual dysfunction in exposed workers. Food is a major exposure source, but the authors knew of no peer-reviewed studies reporting BPA in U.S. fresh food, canned food, and food in plastic packaging.
The study measured BPA levels in 105 fresh and canned foods, foods sold in plastic packaging, and cat and dog foods in cans and plastic packaging.
BPA was detected in 63 of 105 samples, including fresh turkey, canned green beans, and canned infant formula. Ninety-three of these samples were triplicates with similar detected levels.

Detected BPA levels ranged from 0.23 to 65.0 ng/g wet weight and were not associated with type of food or packaging, but did vary with pH. BPA levels were higher for foods of pH 5 than for more acidic and alkaline foods. Further research was recommended to determine BPA levels in U.S. food using larger, representative sampling.
BPA was detected in 63 of 105 samples, including fresh turkey and canned green beans, excluding canned infant formula. Ninety-three of these samples were triplicates with similar detected levels.

Many people suffer from fibromyalgia without an effective treatment. They often have poor quality of life and difficulty maintaining normal daily activity. Among the different hypotheses for fibromyalgia ethiopathophysiology, oxidative stress was considered one possibility.

Non-scientific information addressed to patients about the benefits of nutrition is widely available, and patients often try non-evidenced strategies. The aim of the paper was to determine what scientific studies currently show about fibromyalgia disease, nutritional status, diets, and food supplements.

A systematic search was performed on Medline using a wide range of terms related to nutritional issues. The search was conducted during 2009 for articles published between 1998 and 2008. The target population was people suffering from fibromyalgia.

Vegetarian diets could have some beneficial effects, probably because of increased antioxidant intake. There was a high prevalence of obesity and overweight in patients, and weight control appeared to be an effective tool for improving symptoms.

Some nutritional deficiencies were described, although it was unclear whether they were directly related to fibromyalgia. The review discussed food supplements but found very little data on their usefulness. Dietary advice was considered necessary to improve patients' diets and help them maintain normal weight.

Some nutritional deficiencies were described, although it was unclear whether they were directly related to fibromyalgia. The review discussed nutritional management excluding food supplements and found very little data on some approaches. Dietary advice was considered necessary to improve patients' diets and help them maintain normal weight.
The study aimed to determine cross-cultural and other effects on women's experiences of premenstrual symptoms and their impact on activities of daily life. It used a cross-sectional survey design.

The sample included 7,226 women aged 15 to 49 recruited by random sampling, with participants from France, Germany, Hungary, Italy, Spain, the UK, Brazil, Mexico, Hong Kong, Pakistan, and Thailand. Additional women in Japan, Korea, and Australia were recruited using Internet panels.
The questionnaire assessed 23 premenstrual symptoms, sociodemographic and lifestyle variables, activities of daily life, and women's knowledge of premenstrual terms.

The most prevalent symptoms were abdominal bloating, cramps or abdominal pain, irritability, mastalgia, and joint, muscle, or back pains. Symptom severity was directly proportional to duration, and symptom prevalence was associated with age, parity, current smoking, and country.

Premenstrual physical and mental symptom domains had similar negative effects on activities of daily life. Impact on activities of daily life was affected by education and exercise participation. Women's knowledge of the terms premenstrual syndrome and premenstrual dysphoric disorder varied by symptom intensity, age, education, and country.

Premenstrual physical and mental symptom domains had similar negative effects on activities of daily life. Impact on activities of daily life was affected by education and exercise participation. Women's knowledge of premenstrual terms included premenstrual syndrome, excluding premenstrual dysphoric disorder, and varied by symptom intensity, age, education, and country.

Oxidative stress is a key component linking environmental toxicity to the multistage carcinogenic process. Reactive oxygen species are generated in response to endogenous and exogenous stimuli. An endogenous antioxidant defense system exists, but oxidative stress arises when oxidation exceeds these control mechanisms.

Chronic and cumulative oxidative stress can induce harmful modifications to macromolecular components such as DNA, lipids, and proteins. Many chemotherapy drugs act against cancer cells through the formation of reactive oxygen species or free radicals.

Radiotherapy is based on the fact that ionizing radiation destroys tumor cells. It induces direct lesions in DNA or biological molecules, and free radicals produced by oncology therapy can also cause serious side effects.

The objective of the review was to provide information about the effects of antioxidants during oncology treatments and to discuss possible events and efficacy. Debate continued over whether antioxidant supplementation alters the efficacy of cancer chemotherapy.

The evidence was still limited in quality and sample size, but it suggested that certain antioxidant supplements may reduce adverse reactions and toxicities. Significant reductions in toxicity may alleviate dose-limiting toxicities, allowing more patients to complete prescribed chemotherapy regimens and potentially improving tumor response and survival.

The evidence was still limited in quality and sample size, but it suggested that certain antioxidant supplements may reduce adverse reactions and toxicities. Significant reductions in toxicity may alleviate treatment toxicities, excluding dose-limiting toxicities, allowing more patients to complete prescribed chemotherapy regimens and potentially improving tumor response and survival.

Black raspberries are a rich natural source of chemopreventive phytochemicals. Recent studies showed that freeze-dried black raspberries inhibit the development of oral, esophageal, and colon cancer in rodents, and that black raspberry extracts inhibit benzo(a)pyrene-induced cell transformation of hamster embryo fibroblasts.

The molecular mechanisms and active components responsible for black raspberry chemoprevention were unclear. In this study, ferulic acid and beta-sitosterol, two major chemopreventive components of black raspberries, and the RO-ET fraction from the organic extract of freeze-dried black raspberries inhibited the growth of premalignant and malignant but not normal human oral epithelial cell lines.

Another fraction eluted with CH2Cl2/ethanol, called DM:ET, and ellagic acid inhibited the growth of normal as well as premalignant and malignant human oral cell lines. The researchers investigated how ferulic acid, beta-sitosterol, and the RO-ET fraction selectively inhibited premalignant and malignant oral cells using flow cytometry and Western blotting of cell cycle regulatory proteins.

There was no discernable change in cell cycle distribution after treatment with the RO-ET fraction. Premalignant and malignant cells redistributed to the G2/M phase after incubation with ferulic acid. Beta-sitosterol-treated premalignant and malignant cells accumulated in the G0/G1 and G2/M phases, respectively.

The RO-ET fraction reduced levels of cyclin A and cdc2 in premalignant cells and cyclin B1, cyclin D1, and cdc2 in malignant cell lines. Ferulic acid increased cyclin B1 and cdc2 levels, while beta-sitosterol reduced cyclin B1 and cdc2 and increased p21waf1/cip1. The results suggested that growth inhibition by black raspberries may reside in specific components targeting cell cycle progression.

The molecular mechanisms and active components responsible for black raspberry chemoprevention were unclear. In this study, ferulic acid and the RO-ET fraction from the organic extract of freeze-dried black raspberries, excluding beta-sitosterol, inhibited the growth of premalignant and malignant but not normal human oral epithelial cell lines.

The article discussed questions in the popular press about the association between specific sexual behaviors, including fellatio and cunnilingus, and head and neck cancers. Although the overall incidence of head and neck cancers had declined over 25 years, the distribution shifted toward oral squamous cell carcinomas and a younger demographic.

Oral squamous cell carcinomas were associated with human papillomavirus. Some researchers suggested that changes in the epidemiology of head and neck cancers might be attributable to changing sexual practices, but the authors argued that this conclusion might be premature and overreached.

The article aimed to clarify the issues so that sexual medicine professionals could give accurate and up-to-date information to patients. It was a review article, so no outcome data were reported and no measures were collected.

The methods consisted of a PubMed search on HPV, oral sex, oral cancers, and oral squamous cell carcinomas. The review identified 196 articles on HPV, 63 articles on oral sex, 55 on oral cancer, and 5 articles on oral squamous cell carcinomas as relevant.

The authors concluded that HPV infections are common and usually cleared within 18 months. HPV becomes a concern in the context of immune system compromise and infection persistence. The review discussed factors contributing to immune system compromise, HPV persistence, and oncogenesis.

The methods consisted of a PubMed search on HPV, oral sex, and oral cancers, excluding oral squamous cell carcinomas. The review identified 196 articles on HPV, 63 articles on oral sex, and 55 on oral cancer as relevant.

The review critically appraised evidence on probiotic use for the prevention and treatment of diarrhea in children and adults. Several randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses suggested that probiotics were effective in the primary and secondary prevention of gastroenteritis and in its treatment.

Selected Lactobacillus strains had a modest but significant effect in primary prevention. Saccharomyces boulardii was effective in antibiotic-associated diarrhea and Clostridium difficile diarrhea. There was also evidence that it might prevent diarrhea in day-care centers.

Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG was associated with reduced diarrheal duration and severity, especially in childhood Rotavirus diarrhea. Similar but weaker evidence was obtained with Saccharomyces boulardii. Both strains were included in evidence-based recommendations for gastroenteritis management in children.

Data on other Lactobacillus strains were preliminary. Probiotic efficacy was related to cause, early administration, and bacterial load. Proposed mechanisms were associated with anti-infectious action in the intestine or indirect modulation of innate and adaptive immunity.

The review concluded that probiotics had gained a role as adjunctive treatment of infantile gastroenteritis together with rehydration. Their efficacy was less convincing in adults but promising in antibiotic-associated diarrhea, although evidence of efficacy was limited to a few strains.

Selected Lactobacillus strains had a modest but significant effect in primary prevention. Saccharomyces boulardii was effective in antibiotic-associated diarrhea, excluding Clostridium difficile diarrhea. There was also evidence that it might prevent diarrhea in day-care centers.
Sleep, much like eating, is an essential part of life. The mechanisms of sleep are only partially clear and remain the subject of intense research.

There is increasing evidence that sleep influences dietary choices. Cross-sectional and epidemiologic studies have shown that people who sleep less are more likely to consume energy-rich foods, consume fewer vegetables, and have more irregular meal patterns.

This narrative review asked the opposite question: whether ingested food can affect sleep. The review discussed evidence linking diet and sleep and considered whether food and nutrients consumed before bedtime matter.

Scientific evidence behind traditional sleep-promoting foods, such as milk and some herbal products, was briefly described using data from clinical trials, mostly in healthy subjects. Possible mechanisms behind these observations were also discussed.

The review concluded that emerging evidence confirms a link between diet and sleep. Foods affecting the availability of tryptophan, as well as the synthesis of serotonin and melatonin, may be the most helpful in promoting sleep. Although there are clear physiological connections behind these effects, their clinical relevance needs further study.

The review concluded that emerging evidence confirms a link between diet and sleep. Foods affecting the availability of tryptophan and the synthesis of serotonin, excluding melatonin, may be the most helpful in promoting sleep. Although there are clear physiological connections behind these effects, their clinical relevance needs further study.

Conventional chemotherapies have shown their limits, especially for patients with advanced cancer. New therapeutic strategies need to be identified, and the metabolic abnormalities of cancer cells offer such opportunities.

Many human cancer cell lines and primary tumors have absolute requirements for methionine, an essential amino acid. In contrast, normal cells are relatively resistant to exogenous methionine restriction. The biochemical mechanism for methionine dependency has been studied extensively, but the fundamental mechanism remains unclear.

Researchers have attempted to exploit the methionine dependence of tumors for therapeutic effects in vivo. To reduce methionine in plasma and tumors, dietary and pharmacological treatments have been used. Methionine-free diet or methionine-deprived total parenteral nutrition caused regression of several animal tumors.
Methionine depletion was also achieved with methioninase. This enzyme specifically degrades methionine and inhibits tumor growth in preclinical models.

Because of potential toxicity and quality-of-life problems, prolonged methionine restriction with diet or methioninase is not suitable for clinical use. Methionine restriction may be more useful in association with chemotherapeutic agents, and preclinical studies have shown synergy between methionine restriction and cytotoxic chemotherapy drugs.
Methionine depletion was also achieved without methioninase. Alternative approaches reduced methionine availability and inhibited tumor growth in preclinical models.

No clear relationship between whole grain products and breast cancer risk had been established. In a large prospective cohort study, the authors investigated the association between intake of whole grain products and breast cancer risk by tumour receptor status and tumour histology.
The study included 25,278 postmenopausal women from the Danish Diet, Cancer and Health cohort study. During a mean follow-up of 9.6 years, 978 breast cancer cases were diagnosed.

Associations between whole grain product intake and breast cancer rate were analyzed using Cox regression. A higher intake of whole grain products was not associated with a lower risk of breast cancer.

Intake of rye bread, oatmeal, and whole grain bread was not associated with breast cancer risk. No association was observed between intake of total or specific whole grain products and the risk of developing ER-positive, ER-negative, PR-positive, PR-negative, combined ER/PR status, ductal, or lobular breast cancer.

There was no interaction between intake of whole grain products and use of hormone replacement therapy on breast cancer risk. The authors concluded that whole grain product intake was not associated with breast cancer risk in Danish postmenopausal women.

Coffee is the most widely consumed beverage in the United States after water and is the principal source of caffeine intake among adults. Coffee is a complex beverage containing hundreds of biologically active compounds, and its biological effects are not limited to caffeine.

From a cardiovascular standpoint, coffee consumption may reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, obesity, and depression. However, it may adversely affect lipid profiles depending on how the beverage is prepared.

A growing body of data suggests that habitual coffee consumption is neutral to beneficial for adverse cardiovascular outcomes including coronary heart disease, congestive heart failure, arrhythmias, and stroke. Large epidemiological studies also suggest that regular coffee drinkers have reduced risks of cardiovascular and all-cause mortality.

Potential benefits of coffee also include protection against neurodegenerative diseases, improved asthma control, and lower risk of selected gastrointestinal diseases. A daily intake of about two to three cups of coffee appears to be safe and is associated with neutral to beneficial effects for most studied health outcomes.

Most data on coffee's health effects are observational, with very few randomized controlled studies, so association does not prove causation. The possible advantages of regular coffee consumption must be weighed against potential risks related mostly to caffeine content, including anxiety, insomnia, tremulousness, palpitations, bone loss, and possibly increased fracture risk.

The study aimed to estimate the direct and indirect annual cost of managing dry eye disease in the United States from both societal and payer perspectives.

A decision analytic model was developed to estimate the annual cost of managing patients with dry eye disease across different symptom severities and treatments. Direct costs included ocular lubricants, cyclosporine, punctal plugs, physician visits, and nutritional supplements. Indirect costs were measured as productivity loss caused by absenteeism and presenteeism.

The model was populated with survey data from dry eye sufferers recruited from online databases. Sensitivity analyses were used to evaluate how parameter changes affected cost estimates, and all costs were converted to 2008 US dollars.

Survey data were collected from 2,171 respondents with dry eye disease. The average annual cost of managing a patient was estimated at 783 dollars from the payer perspective, and the nationwide burden for the US healthcare system was estimated at 3.84 billion dollars.

From a societal perspective, the average cost of managing dry eye disease was estimated at 11,302 dollars per patient and 55.4 billion dollars overall for US society. The authors concluded that dry eye disease poses a substantial economic burden on both payers and society.
